The first call (for example after "At start") begins with the first team; when every team has played, the turn number goes up. At the start of each turn the local event "tour_" runs if it exists (e.g. "tour_enemy"). Example: put "Go to the next turn" on the "End turn" button.
- **If it is the turn of…** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Input: Team (tag)  →  Outputs: True / False): True if it is the turn of the team written (its tag), False otherwise. Example: let the player touch their units only during their own turn.
- **Mark as having played** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Input: Object): Remembers that the unit (object A) has played this turn. Everything is cleared when the next turn starts. Example: stop a hero from moving twice in the same turn.
- **If the unit has already played** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Input: Object  →  Outputs: True / False): True if the unit (object A) has already played this turn, False otherwise. Example: refuse to move a hero that has already played.
- **Select the object** (Input: Object): Keeps an object in memory as “the selected object” (for example the chosen unit). Unlike “the involved object”, it does not change when you touch something else: other nodes aim at it with the target “The selected object”. If you don't pick an object, it is the one you just touched. Example: “On click on # unit” then Select the object; then touching a cell moves “The selected object”.
- **Deselect**: Forgets the selected object: nothing is selected anymore (for example when the player cancels, or at the end of the turn). Example: A “Cancel” button: Deselect.
- **If an object is selected** (Outputs: True / False): Checks whether an object is selected. The True output runs if there is one, the False output if not. Example: Touching a cell: if an object is selected, move it; otherwise do nothing.
- **If this object is the selected one** (Input: Object  →  Outputs: True / False): Checks whether the targeted object IS the selected object. Handy to deselect a unit when it is touched a second time. Example: On click on # unit (involved object): if this object is the selected one → Deselect; otherwise → Select.
- **Show reachable cells** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Zone type, Number of steps (or range), Color of the cells, Cell visibility (0 = invisible, 100 = solid), Frame around each cell, Write the step count on each cell, Walls block (movement), These tags block the way (separated by commas), This unit's own costs (tag or terrain name = cost, x = forbidden; e.g. forest=2, Mountain=3, Water=x), Zone name (optional: to show several), Range shape (attack and jump), Minimum range (0 = none; 2 = not the first cells), My positions (column,row; e.g. 2,1 ; -2,1 ; 0,3), Remove the cell the object stands on): Colors the cells the chosen object can move to (or attack). Walls block, and you can add tags that block (other units) and terrains that cost more steps (forest=2). Color, visibility, frame and numbers are adjustable. "Zone name" lets you show several at once (movement in blue, attack in red). Example: show a hero's movement zone when it is touched.
- **Hide the cells** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Input: Zone name (optional)): Clears the colored cells (all of them, or one named zone). Example: hide the zone once the hero has arrived.
- **If the cell is reachable** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Column, Row, Zone name (optional)  →  Outputs: True / False): True if the cell (column, row) is one of the shown cells. By default: the cell the finger touches. False otherwise. Example: refuse a move that is too far with "too far!".
- **Give a unit sheet** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Health points, Attack, Defense, Movement (steps), Attack range (cells), Other statistics (e.g. munitions = 3, armure = 2)): Gives the object its sheet: health, attack, defense, movement and range (object variables "vie", "attaque", "defense", "mouvement", "portee"). They can be read anywhere with a formula, e.g. =hero.mouvement for the number of steps of the reachable cells. Put this node "At start" of each unit, or in a reusable unit prefab. Example: create an archer: health 8, attack 4, defense 0, movement 4, range 3.
- **Attack** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object A, Object B, Attack power (%), Count the defense of the target's terrain, Always at least 1 damage, Destroy the target when its health runs out, Free damage formula (e.g. attacker.attaque * 2 - target.armure); empty = normal calculation, Bonus by target tags (e.g. cavalry = 150, light = 120: % of damage), Bonus by attacker tags (e.g. spear = 130), Statistic used up at each attack (e.g. ammo: no attack at 0), Piercing: % of defense ignored (0 = none), Counterattack: % of the target's attack returned if it survives and the attacker is in its range (0 = none), Height bonus: % damage per level of difference (e.g. 15; higher = more, lower = less), Guard: tag of adjacent allies that strengthen the target's defense (e.g. spear), Guard: defense gained per adjacent ally  →  Outputs: Still alive / Out of health / Attacker destroyed (counterattack)): Object A attacks object B: damage = A's attack × power × bonuses − B's defense − B's terrain defense. Exits “Still alive” and “Out of health” (the target is destroyed if the box is ticked), and “Attacker destroyed” if a counterattack kills it. Both objects need a unit sheet. The “regle: spear > cavalry = 150” rules of donnees.txt apply by themselves. In advanced: bonuses by tags (“cavalry = 150”), PIERCING (percentage of defense ignored, for a spear or a crossbow), COUNTERATTACK (percentage of the target's attack returned if it survives and the attacker is in its range), HEIGHT BONUS (percentage of damage per level of difference: the one higher up hits harder), GUARD (each adjacent ally with the chosen tag adds defense to the target: a shield wall), a free formula, and a statistic used up at each attack (ammo). Example: the spear (piercing 40) against heavy cavalry; the archer on the hill (height +15%).
- **Apply data (unit, weapon)** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Name in donnees.txt (e.g. Knight)  →  Outputs: Found / Not found): Gives object A every value of a unit or weapon written in the donnees.txt file (Assets → Dialogues, or assets_ludexa/Textes/donnees.txt): health, attack, defense, movement, range, price… and its tags. One line is enough: “unite Knight: vie=12, attaque=5, defense=2, mouvement=4, portee=1, tags=cavalry heavy”. You rebalance the game by editing the file, without touching the nodes. Exits “Found” / “Not found”. The file can also hold “arme Sword: attaque=5”, “etat Poison: duree=3, degats=2”, “regle: spear > cavalry = 150” (an attacker tagged spear deals 150% to a target tagged cavalry, applied automatically by “Attack”) and tile heights. Example: at the start of the game, for each hero: Apply data “Knight”.
- **Set tile height** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Start column, Start row, Number of columns, Number of rows, Height (0 = flat)): Gives a height (a level: 0 = flat, 1, 2, 3…) to a rectangle of grid tiles: start column and row, number of columns and rows. Heights drive the height bonus of “Attack” and block sight in the fog of war (a hill hides what is behind it). You can also write them in donnees.txt (“hauteur 3,4 = 2” or a “hauteurs:” block with one digit per tile). Read them with the formula hauteur(column, row) or with the green nodes “Height of the touched tile” / “Height of the tile under an object”. Example: a 3 x 2 tile hill at height 2, so an archer standing on it hits harder.
- **Give a state (poison, slow…)** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, State name (e.g. Poison; set in donnees.txt), Duration in turns (empty = from donnees.txt), Damage each turn (empty = donnees.txt), Statistic changed (e.g. mouvement; empty = donnees.txt), Change to this statistic (e.g. -2)): Gives the unit a state for a number of TURNS: poison (damage every turn), slow (movement drops), blessed (attack rises)… Everything can be written in donnees.txt (“etat Poison: duree=3, degats=2”, “etat Slow: duree=2, stat=mouvement, delta=-2”): then only the state's name is needed. Damage lands at the start of each turn of the unit's team, then the state loses a turn; at the end, the changed statistic goes back to normal. Giving the same state again extends it instead of doubling it. The unit keeps an “etat_” statistic (turns left), readable in a formula. Needs “Go to next turn”. Example: a poisoned arrow: Attack → still alive → give the “Poison” state to the target.
- **Remove a state** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, State name (empty = all)): Removes a state from the unit (by name), or every state if the name is empty. The statistic changed by the state goes straight back to its previous value. Example: a priest who cures an ally's poison.
- **If the unit has the state…** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, State name (empty = all)  →  Outputs: True / False): Tests whether the unit has a state (or any state if the name is empty). Exits “True” / “False”. Example: cannot move if the unit is “Frozen”.
- **Area effect around an object** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Effect, Strength (damage or heal), Radius in tiles, Tags affected (empty = everyone), State name (if the effect gives a state), Falloff per tile of distance (% of strength), Shape, Also hits the object at the centre): Hits every object around object A (at the centre) at once: damage, heal or a state. Settings: the strength, the radius in tiles, the tags affected (empty = everyone), the shape (diamond or square with diagonals), the falloff per tile of distance (explosion: the further away, the weaker), and whether the centre object is hit too. Damage ignores defense. A fireball, a group heal, a scary shout. To count victims in a condition use the formulas compter("tag") and voisins(object, "tag", tiles). Example: a fireball: radius 2, strength 6, falloff 30% per tile, on “enemy” units.
- **Gain experience** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Experience gained, Experience to reach level 2 (x level afterwards), Gains at each level (e.g. vie=2, attaque=1)  →  Outputs: Level up / Nothing to cancel): Gives the unit experience. When it reaches the threshold (threshold × current level) the unit moves up a level, spare experience is kept, and the gains are added (“vie=2, attaque=1”; maximum health rises along with health). The unit keeps the “xp” and “niveau” statistics (1 at the start). Exits “Level up” / “No level up”: play a fanfare or a message when it levels. Example: a hero who gains 30 experience for every enemy defeated.
- **Remember the position** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Input: Object): Remembers the unit's current position, before a move. With “Cancel the move”, the player can go back (as in Advance Wars when you press “Cancel” before acting). Example: just before “Go to tile”: Remember the position.
- **Cancel the move** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Input: Object  →  Outputs: Cancelled / Nothing to cancel): Puts the unit back at the position remembered by “Remember the position”, clears its “has already played” mark and sets its “bouge” and “agi” statistics back to 0. Exits “Cancelled” / “Nothing to cancel”. Example: a “Cancel” button in the unit's action menu.
- **Play like a computer (AI)** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Enemy tags (e.g. player), Play style, Movement speed, Other tags that block the path (e.g. its own allies)  →  Outputs: Arrived / No target): Makes a unit play by itself, like a computer. It looks at where it can go (movement, walls, terrain, blocking units), finds the enemies (their tags) and picks the best tile to attack from according to its STYLE: aggressive (most damage, finishing a target first), cautious (avoids the counterattack) or defensive (likes high-defense tiles). Nobody in range: it moves toward the nearest enemy. Once it arrives, the “Arrived” exit fires: the involved object is the chosen target and the unit's “cible_ia” statistic is 1 (can attack) or 0 (just moved closer). It uses the unit's movement, range (and “portee_min”) and unit sheet. Exit “No enemy” if there are none left. Example: monsters' turn: for each monster, Play like a computer (enemies = player) → on arrival, if cible_ia = 1, Attack.
- **Update the fog of war** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Tags of the team that sees (e.g. player), Tags of enemies to hide when out of sight (e.g. enemy), Default vision in tiles (otherwise the unit's "vision" statistic), Darkness of unknown tiles (0 to 100), Remember tiles already seen): Works out what the team can see and covers the rest of the map with a dark veil: the team's units (tags) see around them up to their “vision” statistic in tiles (otherwise the node's default vision). A terrain wall, a terrain with the property “bloque_vue = oui” (dense forest) or a higher tile stops the view. Tiles already seen stay half dark (memory, optional). Units with enemy tags out of sight are hidden. Run it again after every move or at the start of a turn. The formula vue(column, row) is 1 when the tile is seen. “Remove the fog of war” makes everything visible. Example: at the start of each player turn: Update the fog (team player, enemies enemy, vision 3).
- **Remove the fog of war** [newer than 1.0.1142]: Removes the fog of war: the whole map is visible again and hidden units reappear. Example: at the end of the game, to show the whole map.
- **Give health to the object** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Health points): Gives health points to the chosen object (object variable "vie", and "vie_max" for the maximum). Read it anywhere with a formula, e.g. =monster.vie, to write it in a text or a bar. Example: give a monster 10 health points at the start.
- **Deal damage** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Damage, Destroy the object when its health runs out, Subtract the defense of the terrain it stands on  →  Outputs: Still alive / Out of health): Removes health points from the object (never below 0). Two outputs: "Still alive" and "Out of health" (the object is destroyed if the box is ticked; "the involved object" stays the one hit). Example: a hero hits a monster: 3 damage, then a small message depending on the result.
- **Heal** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Health restored): Gives health points back to the object, without going over its maximum. Example: a potion that restores 5 health points to the hero.
- **Change a statistic** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Statistic name (e.g. ammo), What to do, By how much): Changes a statistic you invented for an object (ammo, armor, mana, fuel…): add to it, subtract from it or set it to a value. If it does not exist yet, it is created at 0. You can then read it anywhere: =archer.ammo. Example: After a shot: Change a statistic → object “archer”, statistic “ammo”, Subtract 1.
- **If the statistic…** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Statistic name (e.g. ammo), Comparison, Value  →  Outputs: True / False): Compares an object's statistic with a value and follows the “true” or “false” exit: for example “ammo is greater than 0”. A statistic that does not exist counts as 0. Example: Before shooting: If the archer's “ammo” statistic is greater than 0 → shoot; otherwise → show “Out of arrows”.
- **Choose a target** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Tags of possible targets (comma-separated), Which target to pick?, Range in cells (0 = unlimited; e.g. =monster.portee), Minimum range (0 = none), Range shape, My positions (column,row; e.g. 2,1 ; -2,1), Statistic (for the “statistic” rules, e.g. defense), Range in pixels, as a circle (0 = use the range in cells)  →  Outputs: Target found / No target): Object A looks among the objects that carry one of the requested tags for those WITHIN ITS RANGE (same shapes as “Show reachable cells”), then picks one: the closest, the one with the least or the most health, or the lowest / highest value of a statistic. “Target found” output: it becomes “the involved object” (for Attack, Go to…). “No target” output: nobody in range. Perfect for the intelligence of a monster or a turret. Example: a monster: “Choose a target” (tag “hero”, the closest, range =monster.range), then “Attack” on “Target found”.
- **Fill the grid** (Inputs: Object, Columns, Rows, Model objects (names separated by commas)): Splits object A (the board) into columns and rows and puts in each cell a copy of a model object picked at random (at least 3 models, names separated by commas). There is never a match at the start, and the pieces drop in from the top. Use it before “Play on the grid (match 3)”. Example: at the start, an 8 x 8 grid of candies "red, orange, yellow, green, blue, pink".
- **Play on the grid (match 3)** (Inputs: Object, Finger X position, Finger Y position  →  Outputs: For each matched piece / Move finished / Swap refused): The heart of a match-3 game (Candy Crush style), to put under “Finger held down”. Touching a piece selects it, touching its neighbour (or sliding the finger to it) swaps them. The swap only stays if it lines up 3 or more identical pieces; otherwise they go back (“Swap refused”). Each matched piece starts “For each matched piece” (the involved object is the piece), then disappears; pieces fall, new ones arrive and combos happen by themselves. When everything is still: “Move finished”. With no possible move, the grid shuffles itself. Example: “For each matched piece”: +10 points and sparkles on the piece; “Move finished”: one move less.
- **Shuffle the grid** (Input: Object): Moves all the pieces of object A's grid to new places, without creating a match and keeping at least one possible move. Example: a "Shuffle" button when the player is stuck.
- **Shuffle places** (Input: Object): Randomly swaps the places of all objects with the chosen tag (Object A = "# tag"). Their child objects follow them. Example: shuffle the cards of a memory game at the start, or the cups of a shell game.

### Values (green wires)

- **Height of the touched tile** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Output: none (end of script)): Green node: the height of the tile the finger touches (0 if nothing is defined). Plug it with 🔗 into a setting, for example in an “If…”. Example: show “Hill!” when a tile of height 2 is touched.
- **Height of the tile under an object** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Input: Object  →  Output: none (end of script)): Green node: the height of the tile under an object. Useful, for example, to compare the attacker's height with the target's. Example: only allow a ranged attack from a tile higher than the target.
- **Random number** (Inputs: From, To  →  Output: none (end of script)): Green node (value): gives a random number between "From" and "To", drawn again each time it is used. Connect it to a setting with the 🔗 button of the settings window. Example: make a coin appear at a random X between 0 and 800.
- **Object value** (Inputs: Object, What  →  Output: none (end of script)): Green node (value): gives a value of the chosen object during the game: its x or y position, width, rotation, opacity… Example: put a coin at the same height as the player (Y ← object value: player, y).
- **Variable value** (Input: Variable  →  Output: none (end of script)): Green node (value): gives the current value of a variable (score, lives…) during the game. Example: show the score in a text (Text ← variable value: score).
- **Calculation** (Inputs: A, Operation, B  →  Output: none (end of script)): Green node (value): calculates A + B, A − B, A × B or A ÷ B. A and B can be numbers, or receive a green wire themselves (chained calculations). Example: give twice as many points (Value ← calculation: score × 2).
- **Touched column** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Output: none (end of script)): Green node (value): gives the column of the cell the finger touches (0 = the first on the left). Plug it into a setting with the 🔗 button. Example: know which column was touched to place a tower.
- **Touched row** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Output: none (end of script)): Green node (value): gives the row of the cell the finger touches (0 = the first at the top). Plug it into a setting with the 🔗 button. Example: know which row was touched to place a building.
- **Object's column** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Input: Object  →  Output: none (end of script)): Green node (value): gives the column of the cell where the chosen object is (0 = the first on the left). Example: know in which column the hero is.
- **Object's row** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Input: Object  →  Output: none (end of script)): Green node (value): gives the row of the cell where the chosen object is (0 = the first at the top). Example: know in which row the hero is.
- **Turn number** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Output: none (end of script)): Green node: the current turn number (1, 2, 3…), plug it in with the 🔗 button. Example: show "Turn 3" in a text.
- **Steps to reach the touched cell** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Output: none (end of script)): Green node: the number of steps to reach the touched cell (-1 if it is outside the zone). Handy to count remaining steps. Example: remaining steps = the unit's steps - this number.
- **Terrain of the touched cell** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Output: none (end of script)): Green node: the name of the terrain of the touched cell ("Forest", "Water"…), or nothing if there is none. Terrains are set in the tile editor. Example: show "Forest" when a forest cell is touched.
- **Terrain cost of the touched cell** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Output: none (end of script)): Green node: the step cost of the terrain of the touched cell (1 if there is none). Example: say "this costs 2 steps" before a move.
- **Terrain under an object** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Input: Object  →  Output: none (end of script)): Green node: the name of the terrain the chosen object stands on. Example: know whether the hero is in water or on the road.
- **Terrain defense under an object** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Input: Object  →  Output: none (end of script)): Green node: the defense bonus of the terrain under the chosen object. Example: show a unit's defense bonus.
- **Distance between 2 objects** (Inputs: Object A, Object B  →  Output: none (end of script)): Green node (value): gives the distance (in pixels) between the centers of two objects during the game. Example: shake the screen harder when the enemy is close.

### Transitions

- **Screen transition (circle, star…)** (Inputs: Shape, Direction, Color, Duration (seconds), Center: object (name; circle, star, diamond, heart, hero)  →  Outputs: Next / Right away): Covers or uncovers the screen with a shape (19 to choose from: circle, star, heart, curtain, clock, checkerboard, swirl…). “Close” covers the screen and it stays covered; “Open” uncovers it. “Next” runs when it's done, “Right away” runs immediately. Example: circle closing → “Go to scene” → circle opening. To change scene in a single step: “Go to scene with a transition”.
- **Go to scene with a transition** (Inputs: Scene, Shape, Color, Closing (seconds), Pause while closed (seconds), Opening (seconds), Shape to reopen, Center: object (name; circle, star, diamond, heart, hero)  →  Output: none (end of script)): Changes scene with a transition: the screen is covered by a shape (circle, star, heart, curtain, swirl… 19 shapes), the new scene arrives, then the screen opens again. There is no output: what happens next is set in “At start” of the new scene. Example: the door is touched: go to the “House” scene with a circle closing on the hero.

### Animations

- **Play animation** (Inputs: Object, Animation, Speed (frames/second), Loop (yes / no)): Plays one of the object's animations, at the chosen speed (frames per second), looping or once. If it is already playing, it continues without restarting. Example: the “walk” animation when the character moves.
- **Stop animation** (Input: Object): Stops the animation and goes back to its first frame. Example: the character stops walking.
- **Pause animation** (Input: Object): Pauses the animation on the current frame. Example: freeze the character during a pause.
- **Resume animation** (Input: Object): Resumes the animation where it was paused. Example: after the pause.
- **Animation speed** (Inputs: Object, Speed (frames/second)): Changes the animation speed (frames per second) without restarting it. Example: running faster = faster animation.

### Audio

- **Play sound** (Inputs: Sound file, Volume (%, 100 = full)): Plays a sound effect. Several sounds can play at the same time. Example: a “bling” when a coin is picked up.
- **Play music** (Inputs: Music file, Loop (yes / no), Volume (%, 100 = full)): Starts a music track, replacing the current one. Do not put it under “Every frame” (it would restart all the time). Example: the level music, at start.
- **Stop music**: Stops the current music. Example: silence on the Game Over screen.

### Story and dialogues

- **Say a line** (Inputs: Who speaks, Emotion, The line, Place on screen, Character entrance, Effect, Sound or voice, Next comes  →  Output: Then): Dialogue game: the chosen character says the line in a dialogue box, letter by letter, and the player taps the screen to continue. The character appears with their emotion (their Character sheet: pictures, color, voice). Special words: [c]color[/c], [t]shake[/t], [o]wave[/o], [p] for a pause, {score} for a variable; "🌐 9 languages" button to translate. Example: Hana (happy) says "Hello!", then “Ask a choice” offers two answers.
- **Ask a choice** (Inputs: Who asks, Emotion, Question (optional), Answer 1, Answer 2, Answer 3, Answer 4, Condition of answer 1, Condition of answer 2, Condition of answer 3, Condition of answer 4, Answer not allowed, Picture for answer 1 (optional), Picture for answer 2 (optional), Picture for answer 3 (optional), Picture for answer 4 (optional), Timer (seconds, 0 = none)  →  Outputs: Answer 1 / Answer 2 / Answer 3 / Answer 4 / Time's up): Shows 2 to 4 answers as big buttons: each answer goes out through its own output, so the story branches like a tree. An answer can require a condition (otherwise it is greyed out or hidden); an optional timer adds the "Time's up" output. Each answer can also have a picture (advanced settings): the answers become big illustrated cards. Example: "Open the treasure" leads to the good ending, "Leave" to the sad one.
- **Change the background** (Inputs: Background image (empty = none), Transition, Slow background movement, Movement duration (seconds), Middle layer, transparent (empty = none), Foreground in front of the characters, transparent (empty = none), Movement distance): Puts a picture as the background, full screen, behind the story's characters (fading or at once). Empty picture = no more background. Example: the meadow at the start, then the forest when Hana goes looking for her cat.
- **Pass through the scenery** (Inputs: Image that passes, Movement (steps), Where does it pass?, Image height (pixels), Image animation (name, optional), Animation speed (frames per second)): Makes an image (bird, cloud, mosquito…) cross the background of a story, following a movement made in Assets → Movement. Choose behind or in front of the characters (the text box always stays on top). “Height” sets the size of the image. If the image is an animation (a bird flapping its wings), type its name in “Image animation” and the speed in “Speed (images per second)”. Example: a bird flying across the sky while Hana talks.
- **Stop the passing images**: Removes all the images currently crossing the story background (started by “Pass through the scenery”). Example: the mosquito leaves when the dialogue is over.
- **Show / hide a character** (Inputs: Character, They…, Emotion, Place on screen, Character entrance): Brings a story character in (emotion, place, entrance: fade, slide, jump), changes their emotion or makes them leave, without speaking. Example: Lyn comes in from the right while Hana is talking.
- **Animate a character** (Inputs: Character, Move to…, Size (100 = normal, 120 = bigger), Number of little jumps, Duration (seconds), Movement style, Shake (it trembles), Wait for the end before continuing): Animates a character already on screen: it slides to another place, grows or shrinks, does little jumps or shakes. You set the duration and the style (even, smooth, quick then soft, slight overshoot, bounce). "Wait for the end" holds the story until the movement is over; otherwise the story goes on while it moves. The character must have been shown first with “Show / hide a character”. Example: Hana slides from left to right with a bounce while she says "Wait for me!".
- **Novel mode (full-screen text)** (Input: What to do?): Switches to "novel mode": the text fills the whole screen over a darkened background and the lines of “Say a line” pile up one under the other, like in a book. When the page is full, it turns by itself. "New page" clears it right away; "Back to the dialogue box" brings back the usual box. Example: A night-time narration in novel mode, then back to the dialogue box for the conversation.
- **SMS mode (phone conversation)** (Inputs: What to do?, Who writes to you (name and photo on top), Who is "me" (their lines on the right), Text under the name (empty = "online")): Shows the conversation as text messages on a phone: the lines of “Say a line” become bubbles (on the left for whoever writes, with three little dots "…" before they appear) and the answers of “Ask a choice” are picked at the bottom of the phone, then arrive on the right. The narrator writes a small caption in the middle (for example "Last night, 10:14 pm"). "Who writes to you" gives the name and photo at the top; "Who is me" makes a character write on the right without going through a choice. "Clear the conversation" empties the phone; "Back to the dialogue box" leaves the mode. Everything is set in the Dialogue style: colours, size, time of the "…", full-screen phone… Example: SMS mode (turn on, who writes to you: Hana) → Say a line (Hana: "Are you there?") → Ask a choice ("Yes, tell me" / "Why?").
- **Unlock an achievement** (Inputs: Achievement name, Description (shown in the list), Achievement image (empty = a star), Hint while it is hidden (empty = none)): Unlocks an achievement: an "Achievement unlocked!" banner slides in at the top of the screen (only the first time in the published game; every time in the editor so you can see it). The achievement joins the "Achievements" tab of "Endings and gallery" of the “Story title screen”: it stays hidden behind "???" (with a hint if you write one) until it is won. Put one at the end of a story, in a secret branch, after “Friendship (hearts)”… The banner is set in the Dialogue style: colours, frame image, time, place (top or bottom), sound. Example: End the story (ending "The lost sock") → Unlock an achievement (name "The lost sock", description "Secret ending found").
- **Replayable scene (gallery)** (Inputs: Start or end of the scene, Scene name (gallery)): Marks a scene the player can watch again from "Endings and gallery" of the “Story title screen” ("Scenes to replay" tab). Put one at the "Start of the scene": when the story passes it, the scene unlocks and the state of the story is remembered. Put another at the "End of the scene": when replaying, the story stops there and goes back to the gallery. Nothing is saved during a replay. Music started with “Play music” also unlocks in the "Music" tab. Example: "The clearing": one node at the start of the meeting with Hana, another right after she leaves.
- **End the story** (Input: Ending name (optional: it counts in "Endings and gallery")): Clears the dialogue box, the characters and the background of the story: the game takes over again. If you give an "Ending name", this ending is remembered forever and counts in "Endings and gallery" of the “Story title screen”; the saved game is erased. Example: "Friends of the cabin" after the last line, then back to the title screen.
- **Friendship (hearts)** (Inputs: Who?, Hearts to add (−1 to remove), Maximum number of hearts): Adds (or removes, with −1) friendship hearts for a character, up to the maximum. The hearts show at the top left during the story and a “+1 ❤” floats up (they can be hidden in the Dialogue style). They are saved with the game and restored by ◀ Back. Example: after the kind answer “I'll stay with you”: Hana +1.
- **If the friendship…** (Inputs: Who?, is, hearts  →  Outputs: True / False): Picks how the story goes on from a character's friendship hearts: the “True” output if the comparison is true, otherwise “False”. For an ending that depends on how you treated the characters. Example: if Hana's friendship is at least 4 → the happy ending, otherwise the sad one.
- **Story title screen** (Inputs: Story title, Background picture (empty = the current background)  →  Output: New game): Shows the story title over a picture, with big buttons: "Continue" (resumes where the player left off, with the background, characters, music and variables: the story saves itself at every line), "New game" (the output: the start of the story) and "Endings and gallery" (endings found and backgrounds already seen, the others are locked). During the story, the ◀ Back button returns to the previous line, even before a choice. Example: placed right after "At start"; every “End the story” comes back to it.
- **Ask the player for a text (name…)** (Inputs: Variable, Question, Suggested answer): Opens a small window with the keyboard: the player types a text (their name…), stored in the chosen variable; it continues when they tap OK. In lines, {prenom} shows this text. Example: "What's your name?" → variable prenom → “Say a line” "Nice to meet you, {prenom}!".

### Screen filters

- **Screen filter** (Inputs: Filter, Strength (%), Fade in (seconds), Duration (seconds, 0 = endless), Keep in the next scene, Also filter buttons and texts (HUD), Flashlight: lit object (name; empty = the one the camera follows), Flashlight: light size (%)  →  Outputs: Then / When it's over): Gives the whole game a “look”, buttons and texts included: TV, VHS, black and white, underwater, nightmare, flashlight… 32 filters to choose from. It fades in gently, stays as long as you want (0 = until you stop it) and can carry on into the next scene. “Then” runs right away, “When it's over” at the end of the duration. Example: the hero is hit: “Hurt” filter for 2 seconds; or “Flashlight” in a cave.
- **Stop the filter** (Input: Fade out (seconds)  →  Outputs: Then / When it's over): Gently fades out the current screen filter. “Then” runs right away, “When it's over” once the filter is gone. Example: the hero leaves the cave: stop the flashlight in 1 second.

### Physics

- **Set the physics world** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Gravity downwards (%, 100 = normal, 0 = space, negative = upwards), Gravity to the right (%, negative = left: a constant wind), Precision, Resting objects fall asleep (lighter on the phone)): Sets the physics world of the scene: gravity downwards (100% = normal, 0 = space, negative = objects fall upwards), sideways gravity (a wind that always blows), calculation precision and whether resting objects fall asleep. Use it once, under “At start”. It only affects objects that have the “Realistic physics” behavior (⚙ Behavior). Example: a level on the Moon: gravity 20%.
- **Adjust a physics object** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Object type, Material (weight, bounce and grip at once), Contact shape, Weight (%, 100 = normal, empty = unchanged), Bounce (0 to 100, empty = unchanged), Grip (0 = ice, 100 = sticky, empty = unchanged), Object gravity (%, 0 = floats, empty = unchanged), Air drag (0 to 20, empty = unchanged), Top speed (pixels per second, 0 = no limit, empty = unchanged), Never rotates, Ghost (things pass through), Very fast object (never goes through a thin wall), Object layer (1 to 8, empty = unchanged)): Changes the settings of a physics object during the game: its type (normal, fixed, guided, or no more physics), material (wood, stone, metal, rubber, ball, ice, feather), shape, weight, bounce, grip, gravity, air drag, top speed, whether it rotates, whether it is a ghost or very fast, its layer. Any setting left empty or on “(do not change)” stays as it is. On an object without physics yet, choosing a type gives it physics. Example: a ball that turns into rubber (material “Rubber”) when a bonus is picked up.
- **Push (physics force)** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Push to the right (negative = to the left), Push downwards (negative = upwards), How, Where to push (off-center, the object starts to spin), Does weight matter?): Pushes a physics object with a force. “Steady push”: repeat it every frame (under “Every frame” or “Finger down”), the object speeds up as long as you push (a rocket, a wind, a fan). “A hit”: adds speed at once (a jump, a kick). By default the effect is the same on a light or heavy object; in the advanced settings you can make weight matter, and push away from the center to make the object spin. Values: pixels per second (per second squared for the steady push). Example: a rocket game: “Finger down” → push upwards (-2500) steadily.
- **Set the speed (physics)** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Speed to the right (pixels per second, empty = unchanged), Speed downwards (negative = upwards, empty = unchanged), Spin speed (degrees per second, empty = unchanged), How, Stop everything at once?): Sets the speed of a physics object, in pixels per second: to the right, downwards (negative = upwards) and spin in degrees per second. Any box left empty leaves that speed unchanged. “Replace” gives exactly this speed; “Add” adds it to the current speed. The “Stop everything” option sets all speeds to zero. Perfect for a jump (downward speed of -900), a sharp stop or a character moving at constant speed. Example: a platformer jump: downward speed = -900, only if “If the physics object…” says the object is standing on something.
- **Launch (angle and speed)** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Angle (degrees: 0 = right, -90 = up, 90 = down, 180 = left), Starting speed (pixels per second), How): Launches a physics object in a direction: you give the angle (0 = to the right, -90 = up, 90 = down, 180 = to the left) and the starting speed. Gravity then does the rest: the object follows a curve. Ideal for a slingshot game, a cannon, a ball throw. The angle can be a formula (for example the angle between the object and the finger). Example: a slingshot: when the finger lets go, launch the bird at the angle of the elastic.
- **Explosion (physics blast)** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Center: X position (empty = at the object's center), Center: Y position (empty = at the object's center), Blast radius (pixels), Force at the center (speed given, pixels per second), Only objects with this tag (empty = all)): Blasts every physics object around a point: the closer to the center, the harder they are thrown, and they start to spin. The center is the middle of the chosen object, or an (x, y) point if you write one. You set the blast radius and the force (the speed given at the center). Option: only objects with a certain tag. The node destroys nothing: combine it with “Particle effect” and “Destroy object” for a real explosion. Example: a bomb: when it touches the ground, explosion with radius 500 and force 1800, then destroy the bomb.
- **Link two objects** (Inputs: Object A, Object B, Kind of link, Link name (to adjust or cut it later), Point of object A where the link is made, Point of object B (rod, spring, rope), Shift the point to the right (pixels), Shift the point downwards (pixels), Do the two objects collide?, Length (pixels, 0 = the starting distance), Spring or suspension stiffness (1 = soft, 10 = firm), Damping (0 to 100: higher means less bouncing), Lower limit (degrees for a hinge, pixels for a slider; empty = none), Upper limit (degrees or pixels; empty = none), Rail or suspension direction (degrees: 0 = horizontal, 90 = vertical; empty = automatic), Motor: speed (degrees per second for a hinge or wheel, pixels per second for a slider; 0 = no motor), Motor or brake strength (1 = weak, 10 = normal, 100 = very strong)): Links two objects so they hold or move together, like in real life. Kind of link: hinge (swings around a point: door, pendulum), rigid rod (fixed distance), spring (elastic, with stiffness), rope (maximum length), slider (slides along a rail, with limits and motor), weld (stuck together), wheel with suspension (car: A = the body, B = the wheel, with motor), brake (top view). Object B is optional: without B, object A is attached to a fixed point of the scenery. Give the link a name to adjust it (“Adjust a link”) or cut it (“Cut a link”) later. In the advanced settings: point on each side, limits, rail direction, motor, collision between the two objects. Both objects need the “Realistic physics” behavior (except a fixed support). Example: a pendulum: A = the ball, B = a small fixed object at the top, type “Hinge” or “Rigid rod”; a bridge: planks linked by hinges.
- **Adjust a link** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Link name, Motor: speed (0 = stop the motor, empty = unchanged), Motor strength (empty = unchanged), Spring or suspension stiffness (empty = unchanged), New length (pixels, empty = unchanged), New lower limit (empty = unchanged), New upper limit (empty = unchanged), Limits): Changes a link already created by “Link two objects” (found by its name): start, stop or speed up its motor, set its strength, the stiffness of a spring or suspension, the length of a rod or rope, the limits. Any empty box stays as before. Example: a car whose wheel motor starts when a button is pressed. Example: “Gas” button: adjust the link “rear_wheel” with motor = 720; on release: motor = 0.
- **Cut a link** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Name of the link to cut, Or: name of an object whose links are all cut): Cuts a link: write its name, or write an object's name to cut all of its links. The objects separate and each falls on its own (a collapsing bridge, a cut rope, a detaching cabin). Example: a trapped bridge: when the hero touches the lever, cut the link “plank_3”.
- **Grab with the finger (physics)** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Action, Only objects with this tag (empty = all), Softness of the grip): Lets you grab a physics object with the finger and drag it, like in real life: the object follows the finger with a bit of elasticity, pushes the others and can get stuck. Put it under “Finger down” (action “Grab and drag”): while the finger is down, the object under it is dragged; as soon as the finger lifts, it is released by itself (or use the “Let go” action). You can restrict the grab to objects with a tag, and set the softness of the grip. Example: a crate puzzle: the player moves crates with a fingertip to build a tower.
- **If the physics object…** [newer than 1.0.1142] (Inputs: Object, Question, Speed from which it counts (pixels per second), Grace time (seconds, for “has just touched the ground”)  →  Outputs: True / False): Asks a question about a physics object and follows the “true” or “false” exit: is it standing on something (to allow a jump), does it touch something, does it touch something above, is it at rest (asleep), is it moving fast, falling, rising. For “moves fast”, “falling” and “rising” the threshold in pixels per second is set in the advanced settings. You can also read values directly in a formula: object.vitesse, object.masse, object.vitesseRotation. Example: a platformer jump: “Jump button” → If the object is standing on something → set downward speed to -900.
